name: Cost Must Drop Dramatically
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: From Tens of Millions to Pocket Change: The Cost Curve Quantum Computing Has Not Found Yet
lesson.summary: Building and running a quantum computer today costs tens of millions of dollars, and unlike classical computing's decades-long collapse in cost per unit of computation, quantum hardware has not yet found an equivalent path to getting dramatically cheaper.
lesson.body:
Recall the infrastructure cost of quantum computing discussed earlier: dilution refrigerators, ultra-pure materials, cleanroom fabrication, specialized cryogenic control electronics, and the small number of engineers and physicists qualified to keep any of it running. Put together, a state-of-the-art quantum computing system today costs tens of millions of dollars to build and a great deal more to operate over its lifetime. That kind of price tag restricts serious quantum computing research to a small number of well-funded companies, national labs, and universities.

Classical computing did not start out cheap either. Early mainframes filled entire rooms and cost the equivalent of millions of dollars, accessible only to governments, universities, and the largest corporations. Over roughly fifty years, a combination of manufacturing standardization, transistor density gains, and enormous consumer demand drove the cost of far more computing power down to the price of a smartphone. That collapse in cost is arguably what made the entire modern software economy possible: cheap, abundant computing let millions of people experiment, build, and fail cheaply.

Quantum computing has not found its version of that curve yet, and there are real reasons to think it will be harder to find. Qubit fabrication yields, the fraction of manufactured qubits that actually work well enough to use, are still low, which means a lot of expensive fabrication gets thrown away. Error correction, covered elsewhere in this course, means a single reliable logical qubit currently requires many physical qubits working together, multiplying the hardware cost of doing anything useful. And unlike classical computing in the 1980s, there is not yet a mass consumer use case creating the kind of manufacturing volume that drives costs down through sheer scale. As an illustrative comparison only, if a machine with enough error-corrected logical qubits to be genuinely useful costs on the order of a billion dollars today, reaching the kind of broad accessibility that cloud classical computing enjoys would require cost reductions on the same rough order of magnitude that took classical computing about half a century to achieve, roughly a millionfold drop in real terms.

Cost is not a side issue, it is a required breakthrough in its own right, because it gates everything else on this list. Manufacturing scale that could bring costs down depends on solving the connectivity, error rate, and yield problems first, since a factory cannot mass produce a design that does not reliably work yet. And low cost is what would let far more researchers iterate on new algorithms, which the previous chapter identified as its own unsolved problem. Cost sits downstream of nearly every other breakthrough, which is part of why it tends to be the last one to fall.
